clinicalPearls: Group of autosomal dominant CMTs defined electrophysiologically by intermediate motor conduction velocities that overlap the demyelinating and axonal ranges
Causative genes include DNM2 (dynamin 2), YARS (tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase), MPZ, INF2 and GDAP1, among others
Clinically resembles classic CMT with distal weakness, wasting, foot deformity and sensory loss
Nerve conduction velocities characteristically fall in an intermediate band, so a single family can show demyelinating-range values in some members and axonal-range values in others
Certain subtypes have distinctive associations, such as neutropenia and cataracts with DNM2 and glomerulopathy with INF2 (as part of a focal segmental glomerulosclerosis phenotype)
The intermediate pattern reflects combined myelin and axonal pathology rather than a single mechanism
Diagnosis requires the intermediate electrophysiology together with confirmation of a pathogenic variant
reference.pathophysiology: Dominant intermediate CMT arises when pathogenic variants affect proteins important to both Schwann cells and axons, so that myelination and axonal integrity are simultaneously compromised. Dynamin 2 (DNM2) participates in membrane trafficking and cytoskeletal regulation; tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase (YARS) is required for protein synthesis and appears to have additional axonal functions; INF2 regulates actin dynamics in both nerve and kidney. Because both the myelin sheath and the axon are affected, conduction slowing is only moderate and response amplitudes are reduced, producing velocities intermediate between the markedly slow demyelinating range and the near-normal axonal range. The mixed pathology also explains the wide intrafamilial variability.
additionalDifferentials: CMT X-linked (GJB1), which also shows intermediate velocities
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies confirming intermediate conduction velocities
Hereditary neuropathy gene panel including DNM2, YARS and INF2
Full blood count for neutropenia and slit-lamp examination for cataract in suspected DNM2 disease
Urinalysis and renal function to detect glomerulopathy in suspected INF2 disease
Detailed pedigree analysis noting dominant inheritance
Exclusion of acquired inflammatory neuropathy when the course is atypical
redFlags: Proteinuria or renal impairment suggesting associated INF2 glomerulopathy
Unexplained neutropenia with infection risk in DNM2-related disease
Subacute worsening pointing to a superimposed acquired neuropathy
Rapidly progressive or asymmetric weakness inconsistent with slowly progressive inherited disease
reference.prognosis: Generally slowly progressive with preserved ambulation in most patients, though severity varies by gene and variant. Associated organ involvement, particularly renal disease with INF2, can influence overall outcome.
pitfalls: Forcing an intermediate result into a purely demyelinating or purely axonal category
Overlooking associated renal disease in INF2-related CMT
Missing haematological or ocular clues to DNM2 disease
Assuming X-linked disease is excluded when intermediate velocities are also typical of GJB1
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy; management centres on physiotherapy to maintain strength and range of movement and prevent contractures
Ankle-foot orthoses, podiatry and orthopaedic care for foot deformity and foot drop, with occupational therapy and assistive devices for hand involvement
Regular monitoring of gait, mobility and distal weakness with ongoing rehabilitation input
Screen for gene-specific associations, including neutropenia and cataract in DNM2 disease and glomerulopathy in INF2 disease using urinalysis and renal function
Avoid neurotoxic drugs that could aggravate the neuropathy
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular team with orthotics, physiotherapy and orthopaedic surgery for correctable deformity
Genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal dominant inheritance
